title: Kissing the leper
hook: Francis writes that what was bitter became sweet

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Benedictine day at home: bell, psalm, work, reading, meal, silence. Your line was balance. Which thing got its hour back? Day one thousand two hundred eight.

Francis of Assisi left a short text now called his Testament, looking back at how it all began. A reader might expect a vision, a voice from heaven, a dramatic call. Instead he starts with his stomach. When he was living in sin, he says, the very sight of lepers was too bitter for him to bear. That's where the story of the Franciscans opens: not with a great deed, but with a man who couldn't stand to look at certain people. Benedict's cloister is behind us now; this is the road, and the friars. Today: kissing the leper.
screen: `FRANCIS LOOKS BACK.` → `NOT A VISION. A REVULSION.` → `OUT OF THE CLOISTER, ONTO THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here is what Francis says happened, in his own Testament. The Lord himself led him among the lepers, and he showed them mercy. And when he left them, what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness, of soul and of body. Then, he says, he waited a little while, and left the world. That's it. A few lines. In his own telling, this is the hinge of his whole life. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't mention a kiss. The kiss comes from the stories his early biographers told. In their telling, Francis is riding near Assisi when he meets a leper on the road. Everything in him wants to turn the horse around. Instead he gets down, gives the man money, and kisses his hand, and the leper kisses him back. In some versions he then goes to the place where lepers lived and serves them there. Two ways of telling it, then: Francis's own spare account, and the vivid scene the biographers drew. Both land on the same turn. Look at who does what in the Testament. Francis doesn't say he conquered his disgust. He says the Lord led him. The change in his feelings came after the mercy, not before it. He didn't wait to feel sweetness before he went. He went, and the bitterness changed on the way out. That's a strange and practical teaching. It suggests that the feeling of revulsion isn't a verdict. It can be the doorway. In the gospels Jesus touches a leper before he heals him. Bitter became sweet.
screen: `THE LORD LED ME AMONG THEM.` · `WHAT WAS BITTER WAS TURNED TO SWEETNESS.` · `THE KISS COMES FROM THE BIOGRAPHERS.` · then, large: `BITTER BECAME SWEET.` · then: `THE FEELING CAME AFTER THE MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing you shrink from. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come to mind that makes you pull back. Not something dangerous. A call you've been avoiding, a person you steer around, a task that turns your stomach a little. Don't argue with the feeling. Just notice where it sits in your body. Then picture yourself doing the thing anyway, gently, slowly, the way Francis got down from his horse. Notice whether the picture changes the feeling at all. If you pray, you can ask to be led, the way Francis says he was. The bell holds the time.
Kissing the leper. The turning point Francis described in his Testament: what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness, once he showed mercy. Today's word.
Your line: bitter became sweet. Today, do the one thing you shrink from, early, before the feeling has time to grow. Day one thousand two hundred eight.

howItsDone: Franciscans tell the story of the leper as the start of Francis's conversion, and Franciscan friars and sisters still serve the sick and the poor in hospitals, shelters and missions.

fork.setup: you're Francis, riding near Assisi. a leper is on the road ahead, and everything in you wants to turn the horse around. what do you do?
options: toss him a coin from the saddle.
get down, give him money, and kiss his hand.
fork.reveal: in the biographers' telling he dismounts, gives the man money and kisses him. in his own Testament, he simply says the bitter became sweet.

original.note: Latin: sweetness, the word Francis's Testament uses for what the bitterness became.

trapdoor: what you thought: Francis was a gentle saint who loved everyone easily.
what it means: he says the sight of lepers was too bitter to bear, until he was led to show them mercy.
what a scholar hears: the Testament never mentions a kiss; that detail comes from the early lives of Francis.

sources.work: The Writings of Saint Francis of Assisi

notes: The Testament is paraphrased: 'when I was in sins, it seemed too bitter to me to see lepers; the Lord himself led me among them and I showed mercy to them; and when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me was changed into sweetness of soul and body; afterward I waited a little and left the world.' Confirm the paraphrase.

The leper meeting with the kiss: Celano's Second Life 9 and Bonaventure's Major Legend 1.5 (and Celano's First Life 17 on serving lepers). Confirm references and details (dismounting, money, kiss of the hand, leper's kiss in return).
'Francis's first followers would come to spend time serving lepers' — confirm (Earlier Rule ch. 9 speaks of friars living among lepers).
Latin of the Testament: 'conversum fuit mihi in dulcedinem animi et corporis' — confirm 'dulcedo' and its pronunciation (ecclesiastical Latin).
Mark 1:40–42 paraphrased: Jesus touches the leper before healing him.
